tldr: We propose Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG), a method that stabilizes high-variance gradients in differentiable simulation with stiff contacts by locally running and averaging parallel rollouts with small perturbations only when contacts occur. This enables learning dynamic humanoid motions with more than an order of magnitude fewer samples than PPO, achieving the world's first zero-shot transfer of a differentiable simulation policy onto a real Unitree G1 humanoid.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG) method. (a) Dynamic motions of the Unitree G1 learned in a differentiable simulation maintaining stiff contacts. (b) At time $t$ when stiff contact is detected, $B$ branches with contact foot positions and velocities sampled from a small perturbation ball are simulated in parallel for $H$ steps, and their states are averaged. During backpropagation, while gradients along individual branches diverge sharply at contact, their bundled average aligns directions and dramatically reduces gradient variance. (c) Zero-shot deployment of the learned policy onto the physical G1 humanoid platform.
overview:
Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) methods like PPO have long been the dominant approach for learning motions on high-dimensional, underactuated, contact-rich robots such as humanoids. However, treating the underlying physics as a black box makes them notoriously sample-inefficient, demanding billions of simulated steps and massive wall-clock training time. To address this, first-order policy optimization using differentiable simulation—which provides analytic gradients through the dynamics to optimize policies directly—has attracted strong interest.

Yet, a major hurdle remained. In differentiable simulation, obtaining smooth gradients typically requires softening the contact model (e.g., lowering penalty stiffness). This produces unrealistic artifacts, such as feet deeply penetrating the ground, which fail to transfer to real robots. Conversely, introducing stiff contact dynamics suitable for real-world deployment makes the physics hyper-sensitive to tiny state perturbations, causing gradient variance to explode and destabilizing policy learning.

To break this trade-off, the authors introduce Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG), a contact-local randomized smoothing framework. Instead of smoothing entire trajectories, BCG triggers only at the exact moments stiff contact occurs: it spawns a local bundle of small perturbed rollouts in parallel on the GPU and averages their states. The forward pass preserves stiff physical realism, while backpropagation averages gradients across the bundle to cancel out extreme variance.

Experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid show that BCG learns dynamic motions—including running, jumping, and dancing—using over an order of magnitude fewer samples than PPO. Furthermore, it achieves the world's first zero-shot transfer of a policy trained in a differentiable simulator onto a physical humanoid robot.
contributions: Proposing Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG), a contact-local randomized smoothing framework that reduces gradient variance without softening stiff contact dynamics.

Combining first-order policy optimization (SHAC) with differentiable imitation rewards from Adversarial Differential Discriminators (ADD) for the first time, achieving precise motion tracking without manual reward weight tuning.
Achieving comparable or superior tracking performance to PPO with over an order of magnitude fewer environment samples and reduced training time.
Demonstrating the world's first zero-shot transfer of dynamic humanoid motion policies trained via differentiable simulation onto a real-world Unitree G1 platform.

sections.heading: Why is differentiating through stiff contacts so hard?
sections.summary: Differentiable simulation offers high sample efficiency, but stiff contact dynamics required for real-world deployment cause gradient variance to explode. This paper proposes BCG, which runs localized parallel perturbation rollouts only when stiff contact occurs to stabilize gradients, achieving zero-shot transfer to a physical humanoid.
sections.details:
Model-free reinforcement learning (RL), such as PPO, has been the go-to approach for training agile locomotion and whole-body humanoid behaviors. Because it does not require differentiating physics, it handles non-smooth contact models reliably. However, relying on zeroth-order gradient estimation leads to poor sample efficiency, burning billions of simulation steps and massive computational time.

In contrast, first-order policy optimization backpropagates analytic gradients through differentiable simulator dynamics. This provides lower gradient variance and dramatically higher sample efficiency. Yet most prior successes stayed confined to simulation due to a contact stiffness dilemma. Softening contacts produces smooth gradients but yields unphysical motions, such as deep ground penetration, causing policies to fail on physical hardware. On the other hand, setting stiff contacts suitable for real-world deployment makes gradients hyper-sensitive to small state shifts, leading to exploding variance and optimization failure.

To solve this, the authors introduce Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG). Rather than smoothing entire trajectories, BCG activates only at localized steps where stiff contacts are detected. It injects small Cartesian perturbations at the contact foot, rolls out a bundle of perturbed branches in parallel on the GPU for a few steps, and averages them. This preserves stiff physical behavior on the forward rollout while providing stable, averaged gradients during backward propagation.

sections.heading: How prior work tackled the contact gradient challenge
sections.summary: Previous efforts to make contacts differentiable have explored soft contact models, complementarity formulations (LCP/NCP), trajectory truncation, and randomized smoothing. BCG builds on these ideas by applying randomized smoothing locally around stiff contacts specifically tailored for first-order RL.
sections.details:
### II-A Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Robot Control
Model-free RL methods like PPO are robust to contact discontinuities and have achieved significant success in Sim-to-Real transfer for legged robots. However, for high-dimensional humanoids, high gradient variance makes their sample inefficiency a major bottleneck.

### II-B Differentiable Simulation and First-Order Policy Optimization
With the rise of GPU-accelerated differentiable physics engines (such as NVIDIA Warp), efficient algorithms like SHAC (Short Horizon Actor-Critic) were developed to backpropagate gradients over short horizons. While initial Sim-to-Real transfers have appeared on quadrupeds, humanoids have much smaller stability margins and demand significantly higher contact fidelity.

### II-C Difficulties of Gradient Propagation Through Stiff Contacts
Contact models generally split into penalty-based (soft) and complementarity-based (rigid) approaches. Stiff penalty methods degrade gradient accuracy under finite time steps. Implicit differentiation via interior-point methods for complementarity problems (LCP/NCP) is difficult to parallelize and vulnerable to local minima. Truncating gradients at contact (like AHAC) prevents gradient explosion or vanishing, but discards vital sensitivity information across contact phases.

### II-D Randomized Smoothing and Bundled Gradients for Contact
In trajectory optimization, randomized smoothing and bundled gradients average gradients over perturbed samples. However, applying them globally across entire trajectories is computationally prohibitive. BCG makes this practical for first-order RL by applying bundling locally, only at the moments stiff contact events take place.

sections.heading: Background: RL, Differentiable Simulation, and SHAC
sections.summary: This section covers reinforcement learning fundamentals, gradient propagation in differentiable simulators, analytically smoothed contact models, and SHAC. Increasing the contact stiffness parameter $\kappa$ improves physical fidelity, but sharpens gradient sensitivities drastically.
sections.details:
### III-A Reinforcement Learning
To maximize the expected return of policy $\pi_\theta(a_t \mid x_t)$, model-free RL uses likelihood-ratio policy gradients (REINFORCE / PPO). Because it does not use physics derivatives, it is robust to contact discontinuities, but gradient variance grows rapidly with longer horizons and higher action dimensions.

### III-B Differentiable Simulation
When the simulator transition dynamics $x_{t+1} = f_\kappa(x_t, a_t)$ are differentiable, the chain rule can be applied directly through trajectory rollouts to compute analytic first-order policy gradients $\nabla_\theta J$. This drastically reduces gradient variance and improves sample efficiency. However, increasing contact stiffness $\kappa$ makes the dynamics Jacobians extremely sensitive, causing variance to resurface.

### III-C Analytically Smoothed Contact Model
This work adopts a Moreau time-stepping formulation where contact impulse is modulated by a smooth sigmoid-like scaling function $s(d) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\kappa d)}$ based on penetration depth $d$. This allows impulses to ramp up smoothly prior to contact. Large, finite values of $\kappa$ approximate rigid contact, and BCG stabilizes gradient flow under these large values of $\kappa$.

### III-D First-Order Policy Optimization via SHAC
To prevent gradient explosion and vanishing over long horizons, SHAC backpropagates gradients through short $N$-step rollouts and bootstraps terminal values using a learned critic $V_\psi$. Even within these short horizons, however, stiff contact dynamics still trigger disruptive gradient spikes.

sections.heading: Proposed Method: Taming Stiff Contact Gradients with Local Bundles
sections.summary: BCG activates only when normal contact impulse exceeds a threshold. It adds small Cartesian position and velocity perturbations to the contact foot, rolls out $B$ branches in parallel for $H$ steps, and averages their states. Automatic differentiation across these branches averages the Jacobians, producing stable, low-variance gradients.
sections.details:
The BCG framework consists of three core phases alongside an imitation learning objective:

### IV-A Contact-Local Perturbations
At step $k$, bundling is triggered when the normal contact impulse exceeds threshold $\tau$ (set to 400 N, exceeding the robot's weight). For the end-effector (foot) of the contacting leg, small position ($\sigma_p = 1$ cm) and velocity ($\sigma_v = 2$ cm/s) offsets are sampled from Gaussian distributions in Cartesian space. Using the damped pseudoinverse Jacobian $J_k^\dagger$, these are mapped to joint-space increments $\Delta q^{(i)}, \Delta \dot{q}^{(i)}$ to create $B$ perturbed states $x_k^{(i)}$. Sampling is treated as a constant operation, so the sampling process itself is not differentiated during backpropagation.

### IV-B Multi-Step Bundled Rollout
The generated $B$ branches are propagated in parallel on the GPU for $H$ control steps ($H=2$) under the common policy action $a_k$. Each control step contains multiple internal simulation sub-steps ($S$ sub-steps). At the end of each step, positions and velocities are arithmetically averaged to form the aggregated state $\bar{x}_{t+1}$. For $t > k$, the next action $a_t = \pi_\theta(\bar{x}_t)$ is queried from this mean state and broadcast across all branches. After $H$ steps, the rollout resumes as a standard single trajectory from the averaged state.

### IV-C Gradient Propagation
In a single rollout, backpropagation propagates sharp Jacobians via $Z_{t+1} = F_{x,t} Z_t + F_{a,t} U_t$. In BCG, sensitivities across all branches are averaged:
$$\bar{Z}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \left( F_{x,t}^{(i)} Z_t^{(i)} + F_{a,t}^{(i)} U_t \right)$$
This averaging acts as a local smoothing operator, canceling out extreme gradient spikes caused by stiff contacts.

### IV-D Policy Optimization with Imitation Objectives
For imitation learning, the method uses Adversarial Differential Discriminators (ADD). Rewards are computed by passing feature residuals against reference motions through a differentiable discriminator $D_\varphi$. This removes the need for manual tracking reward tuning and allows gradients to backpropagate end-to-end from the reward function, through physics, directly into the policy.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: An Order-of-Magnitude Boost in Sample Efficiency and Real Humanoid Deployment
sections.summary: Evaluations across four dynamic motions (run, jump, fight, dance) on the Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrated that contact stiffness is essential for transfer, and that BCG drastically reduces gradient variance. BCG achieved high tracking accuracy with over an order of magnitude fewer samples than PPO and enabled successful zero-shot transfer to the real robot.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations used the Unitree G1 humanoid targeting four dynamic 15-second motions from the LAFAN1 dataset: Run, Jump, Fight, and Dance. A differentiable rigid-body simulator built on NVIDIA Warp was used with rollout horizon $N=32$, bundle size $B=10$, and bundle duration $H=2$. Policies were evaluated in Sim-to-Sim transfer using MuJoCo and Sim-to-Real deployment on the physical G1.

### V-B 1 Q1: Impact of Contact Stiffness on Transfer
Policies trained with varying contact stiffness $\kappa$ were transferred to MuJoCo. Policies trained with low stiffness (soft contact) suffered repeated falls because MuJoCo did not reproduce the artificial foot penetration (Table 1). Increasing $\kappa$ reduced fall counts, confirming that stiff contacts during training are critical for real-world transfer.

### V-B 2 Q2: Gradient Variance and Sensitivity Reduction
Measuring policy gradient variance across parallel environments at a Jump training checkpoint revealed that BCG substantially suppressed variance. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of state gradient vectors for pelvis vertical velocity showed that individual branch gradients (orange dots) were widely scattered, while bundled gradients (blue dots) tightly clustered, proving that contact-induced gradient turbulence is effectively mitigated.

### V-B 3 Q3: Training Efficiency and Convergence
In learning curve comparisons, SHAC+BCG reached high reward levels using 10x to 20x fewer samples than PPO. Standard vanilla SHAC stalled mid-training due to gradient explosion under stiff contacts. While bundling adds slight per-step computational overhead, its informative gradients allowed cutting parallel environments in half (from 128 to 64), leading to superior overall training efficiency.

### V-B 4 Q4: Tracking Accuracy Comparison
Whole-body link tracking errors after transfer to MuJoCo (Table 2) showed SHAC+BCG outperforming PPO on three out of four motions. While PPO had slightly lower numerical error on Jump, visual inspection revealed that PPO gave up jumping entirely, staying standing with both feet on the ground. Only BCG, leveraging first-order gradients, faithfully tracked the jump.

### V-B 5 Q5: Sim-to-Real Transfer on Physical Humanoid
Policies trained with SHAC+BCG were deployed zero-shot onto the physical Unitree G1 without any real-world calibration or fine-tuning. The physical robot successfully and stably reproduced the dynamic motions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: BCG stabilizes analytic gradients using contact-local randomized smoothing while preserving stiff contact physics. It enables dynamic humanoid motion learning with exceptional sample efficiency and achieves zero-shot real-world deployment. Future directions include parameter adaptation and whole-body manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG), a method that stabilizes first-order policy optimization while maintaining stiff contact dynamics necessary for real-world deployment. By launching and averaging local perturbation branches only during contact events, BCG sharply curtails gradient variance without sacrificing physical fidelity.

Combined with SHAC and ADD, the method masters dynamic humanoid skills with more than an order of magnitude fewer samples than PPO, accomplishing the first zero-shot transfer from a differentiable simulator onto a physical humanoid robot.

Future work includes lowering computational overhead during prolonged, continuous contact phases and dynamically adapting perturbation scales $\sigma$ and bundle counts $B$ based on local contact sensitivity. Furthermore, extending the approach beyond locomotion to whole-body loco-manipulation and dexterous hand manipulation represents an exciting next step.

takeaways: Keeping forward physics stiff while smoothing gradients locally during backpropagation is key to overcoming the Sim-to-Real gap and gradient explosion trade-off.
While global randomized smoothing across entire trajectories is computationally prohibitive, bundling locally at contact impacts for a few GPU steps keeps overhead practical.

First-order gradients from differentiable simulators (SHAC), paired with gradient stabilization and differentiable rewards (ADD), can achieve over 10x the sample efficiency of PPO alongside superior motion fidelity.
Policies learned via differentiable simulation can transfer zero-shot to physical humanoids, provided contact stiffness is maintained at realistic levels during training.
limitations: In tasks with persistent, uninterrupted contacts (e.g., continuous heavy-duty manipulation), bundling may trigger continuously, increasing computational and memory costs beyond PPO.
Perturbation parameters (position 1 cm, velocity 2 cm/s) and bundle size (10 branches) are fixed hyperparameters that require manual tuning for different robots or tasks.
The framework relies on an analytically smoothed contact model with finite stiffness $\kappa$ and cannot be applied directly to strictly discontinuous, rigid LCP formulations.
